technique.how: Curvilinear probe, patient supine. Trace the aorta in transverse from the xiphoid (celiac/SMA level) to the bifurcation, measuring maximal outer-wall to outer-wall diameter at proximal, mid, and distal segments, then confirm in a longitudinal view; bowel gas is displaced with steady graded pressure. Diameter >=3.0 cm at any level is positive.
technique.prerequisites: Trained operator; the entire aorta from diaphragm to bifurcation must be visualized for a negative study.
technique.contraindications: None; do not delay resuscitation or surgical consultation for a complete scan in an unstable patient with a clearly aneurysmal aorta.

interpretation.positive_finding: Aortic diameter >=3.0 cm on ED ultrasound has pooled specificity 98% and identifies AAA reliably; in a symptomatic patient this is presumed rupture until CT (if stable) or the operating room proves otherwise.
interpretation.negative_finding: A fully visualized aorta <3.0 cm throughout has pooled sensitivity 99% and effectively excludes AAA as the cause of symptoms; an incompletely visualized aorta is indeterminate, not negative.
interpretation.pitfalls: Ultrasound does not detect rupture itself (retroperitoneal blood is rarely seen) and misses only where the aorta is not visualized; mistaking the IVC or a tortuous aorta for aneurysm, measuring inner wall only, or obliquely cutting the vessel gives errors. Bowel gas and obesity limit views.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive with symptoms: immediate vascular surgery consult and resuscitation (CT only if stable); negative with complete visualization: pursue other causes of pain/hypotension.

estimates.target_condition: AAA (aortic dilation >=3 cm) by emergency-physician bedside ultrasound
estimates.population: Adult ED patients with suspected AAA; 7 studies, 655 patients; emergency physician operators
estimates.reference_standard: CT, MRI, aortography, radiology-performed ultrasound, radiology over-read of ED US, laparotomy, or autopsy
estimates.quote: sensitivity 99% (95% confidence interval [CI] = 96% to 100%) and specificity 98% (95% CI = 97% to 99%)

estimates.target_condition: AAA detection by non-radiologist performed ultrasound
estimates.population: 11 studies, 944 patients; non-radiologist operators (emergency physicians, surgeons, primary care, others) in screening and symptomatic settings
estimates.reference_standard: Radiologist-performed aortic imaging, intra-operative, or post-mortem findings
estimates.quote: NRPUS had a pooled sensitivity of 0.975 [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.942-0.992] for AAA detection and a pooled specificity of 0.989 (95% CI, 0.979-0.995)

sources.citation: Rubano E, Mehta N, Caputo W, Paladino L, Sinert R. Systematic review: emergency department bedside ultrasonography for diagnosing suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm. Acad Emerg Med. 2013;20(2):128-138.

Concannon E, McHugh S, Healy DA, et al. Diagnostic accuracy of non-radiologist performed ultrasound for abdominal aortic aneurysm: systematic review and meta-analysis. Int J Clin Pract. 2014;68(9):1122-1129.
Lederle FA, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Does this patient have abdominal aortic aneurysm? JAMA. 1999;281(1):77-82.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not call a study negative unless the entire aorta was visualized; do not use ultrasound to exclude rupture in a patient with a known AAA and compatible symptoms.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: AAA >=3 cm with pain, hypotension, or syncope: treat as rupture; activate vascular surgery and transfuse/resuscitate without waiting for CT if unstable.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Pooled estimates showed no significant heterogeneity across studies (Concannon 2014); non-diagnostic/incomplete studies were excluded or counted variably across primary studies.
safety_scope.skill_assumption: Emergency physician or hospitalist with focused aortic ultrasound training (included studies used credentialed ED sonographers or physicians after short courses); performance assumes complete aortic visualization from diaphragm to bifurcation.

extraction_notes: Both estimates are from meta-analysis abstracts; full-text tables were not accessible (neither is in PMC), so LRs were not computed and per-study prevalence is given only for the Rubano ED cohort (23% weighted average in symptomatic patients >50 years). Rubano 2013 defines AAA as >=3 cm and restricts to ED bedside ultrasound; Concannon 2014 includes non-ED non-radiologist operators and is listed separately. Lederle 1999 cited as index RCE for palpation vs ultrasound.
